extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and theoretical researchers preparing research papers (authors of math papers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting the opening of a mathematics research paper so readers are prepared: establish context, motivate results, and choose an opening style appropriate to the paper's story. Focused on how to write the foreword/introduction and when to use a direct statement of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish context and motivation before results
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than jumping directly to results, prepare readers by establishing context and motivation first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core principle: set up the problem, why it matters, and the intuition before stating main theorems. This prepares readers who may not share the author's immediate perspective and makes the contribution meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write a Foreword
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a paragraph or two devoted to philosophy underlying your work or a high level explanation of the key idea before stating main results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place a short foreword at the start that gives the paper's guiding philosophy or the key idea in plain language. This is meant to orient the reader prior to formal statements and technical details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the opening literary and memorable
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider putting in the Foreword some highly literary description of what you are doing. If it's beautiful or sufficiently memorable, it might be quoted in other papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid, memorable phrasing where appropriate to make the paper stand out; a well-crafted line can be reused by others. Balance literary flair with clarity—don't sacrifice accuracy for ornament.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss the big picture
rubrics_metrics.description: Cover motivational examples, general physical or philosophical principles, and connections to other fields — 'there is no other place in the paper to do this.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the opening to situate the work within broader contexts, give motivating examples, and highlight interconnections. Treat the introduction as the sole place to do wide-ranging exposition and cross-field connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use compelling openings (choose an evocative frame)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open with engaging frames such as the nature of the field and its tools; classical context paired with modern developments; philosophical puzzles underlying the work; or relationships between different mathematical areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select an opening style that best showcases your paper's story—examples provided (field nature, historical context, philosophical puzzle, inter-area relationships) can guide tone and content of the introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct 'get to the point' only when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Get to the point' only succeeds for simple stories — e.g. resolving a famous conjecture where readers already understand the background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve the terse, direct statement-of-results approach for papers whose story is simple and for an audience already familiar with the background. For most papers, an explanatory lead-in is preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signal the paper's type at the outset
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good' paper signals at the outset which kind of paper it is — a famous-conjecture closure or a context-laden story — and writes the opening to match.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear early whether the paper is primarily a dramatic result that needs little exposition or a conceptual contribution that requires broader motivation; match tone and structure of the opening to that signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid emulating amusing but inappropriate examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Some examples in the post are 'for amusement purposes and definitely not [to] be emulated.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise judgement: humorous or exaggerated example openings can illustrate a point but may not suit your paper; do not blindly copy playful or gimmicky openings if they undermine clarity or credibility.
